title: Budgets and Budgetary Control
outcomes: Explain budgets, budgetary control and the budget process.
Prepare flexible budgets and compute budget ratios.

meta.exam_tip: Start every budget question with the principal budget factor and the sequence of budgets.

concepts.title: Budgets, budgetary control and the budget process
body: A budget is a quantitative plan, prepared in advance for a defined period, of income, expenditure and resources needed to achieve objectives. Budgetary control sets budgets for responsibility centres, compares actuals continuously and acts on deviations.

The process: set objectives; identify the principal budget factor (key factor) that limits activity — often sales, sometimes materials, labour or capacity; prepare functional budgets in sequence; consolidate into the master budget; monitor and revise.

Organisation: a budget committee coordinates, a budget officer manages, and a budget manual sets procedures. Benefits: planning, coordination, control and motivation; limitations: estimates may be inaccurate, rigidity, and cost of the system.
concepts.analogy: A budget is a plan in numbers; budgetary control is using it to steer.
concepts.work: If a factory can sell more than it can make, capacity — not sales — is the principal budget factor.

concepts.title: Functional budgets
body: Sales budget (quantity and value by product and region) leads to the production budget: production = sales + closing finished stock − opening finished stock.

Materials: requirement = production × usage per unit; purchases = requirement + closing material stock − opening material stock. Labour budget = production × hours per unit × rate. Overhead budgets for production, administration, selling.

The cash budget lists expected receipts and payments month by month to show surpluses or shortages; it excludes non-cash items like depreciation. All functional budgets feed the master budget (budgeted P&L and balance sheet).
concepts.analogy: Each budget is built from the one before, starting from sales.
concepts.work: Selling 5,000 units with stock rising by 500 means producing 5,500 units.

concepts.title: Fixed and flexible budgets; budget ratios
body: A fixed budget is set for one level of activity; it is fine where activity is stable but misleading for control when actual output differs.
A flexible budget adjusts costs to the actual level of activity by separating fixed, variable and semi-variable costs; it allows like-for-like comparison.

Ratios: efficiency ratio = standard hours for actual output ÷ actual hours × 100; activity ratio = standard hours for actual output ÷ budgeted hours × 100; capacity ratio = actual hours ÷ budgeted hours × 100. Activity = efficiency × capacity. The calendar ratio compares available working days with budgeted days.
concepts.analogy: Compare actual cost with what cost should have been at the actual level, not at the planned level.
concepts.work: Budgeted 10,000 hours; worked 9,000; standard hours for output 9,900: efficiency 110%, capacity 90%, activity 99%.

concepts.title: Zero-based and performance budgeting
body: Zero-based budgeting (ZBB) builds every budget from zero each period: each activity is identified as a decision package, evaluated on cost and benefit, ranked and funded by priority — rather than adding a percentage to last year's figure.
ZBB avoids carrying forward inefficiency but is time-consuming; it suits service and support functions and Government programmes.

Performance budgeting links spending with physical outputs and results (programmes, activities, targets) — widely used in the public sector; outcome budgeting goes further to measure results achieved.
concepts.analogy: ZBB asks "why spend at all?", not "how much more than last year?".
concepts.work: A training department under ZBB must justify each programme instead of receiving last year's budget plus 10%.

illustrations.title: From sales to purchases
illustrations.q: Budgeted sales 12,000 units. Finished goods: opening 2,000, desired closing 2,500. Each unit needs 3 kg of material at ₹20/kg; material stock: opening 5,000 kg, desired closing 6,000 kg. Prepare the production budget and the material purchase budget.

illustrations.title: Flexing the budget
illustrations.q: At 100% capacity (10,000 units): variable cost ₹50/unit; semi-variable overheads ₹1,00,000 (40% fixed); fixed overheads ₹2,00,000. Prepare a flexible budget at 60% and 80% capacity, with cost per unit.

solution.text: Cost per unit falls as volume rises because fixed costs are spread over more units.

jobs.title: Cash budget for a festive season
jobs.situation: A retailer expects heavy purchases in September and collections in November.
steps: Estimate monthly sales and collection pattern.
jobs.takeaway: Profitable businesses can still run out of cash — the cash budget shows when.

options: The factor that limits the organisation's activity
mcqs.explain: Also called key or limiting factor; often sales, but may be materials, labour or capacity. In practice: identify it first.
mcqs.topic: Budgets, budgetary control and the budget process

mcqs.q: Sales 10,000 units; opening FG 1,500; closing FG 1,000. Production:
mcqs.explain: 10,000 + 1,000 − 1,500 = 9,500. In practice: stock reduction lowers production.

mcqs.q: A cash budget does NOT include:
mcqs.explain: Depreciation is non-cash. In practice: capital purchases do appear when paid.

mcqs.q: A flexible budget is useful because it:
options: Adjusts costs to the actual level of activity
Is set for one level only
mcqs.explain: It compares actual cost with allowed cost for the same activity. In practice: it needs fixed/variable split.
mcqs.topic: Fixed and flexible budgets; budget ratios

mcqs.q: Standard hours for actual output 4,400; actual hours 4,000. Efficiency ratio:
mcqs.explain: 4,400 ÷ 4,000 × 100 = 110%. In practice: above 100% means better than standard.
mcqs.topic: Fixed and flexible budgets; budget ratios

mcqs.explain: Activity = (SH/BH) = (SH/AH) × (AH/BH). In practice: use to check workings.
mcqs.topic: Fixed and flexible budgets; budget ratios

options: Requires each activity to be justified from zero
Adds inflation to last year's budget
Is the same as a fixed budget
mcqs.explain: ZBB evaluates decision packages afresh. In practice: costly but sharpens spending.

mcqs.q: Semi-variable cost ₹80,000 at 100% (25% fixed). At 75% activity it is:
mcqs.explain: Fixed 20,000 + variable 60,000 × 75% = 45,000 → total 65,000. In practice: split semi-variable costs first.
mcqs.topic: Fixed and flexible budgets; budget ratios

At 100% capacity (10,000 units): variable cost ₹50/unit; semi-variable overheads ₹1,00,000 (40% fixed); fixed overheads ₹2,00,000. Prepare a flexible budget at 60% and 80% capacity, with cost per unit.

model.text: Cost per unit falls as volume rises because fixed costs are spread over more units.

summary: Principal budget factor drives the sequence.
Production = sales + closing FG − opening FG; purchases = usage + closing − opening material.
Flexible budget: split fixed, variable, semi-variable.
Efficiency = SH/AH; capacity = AH/BH; activity = SH/BH.
traps: Depreciation never appears in a cash budget.

viva.model: Setting budgets for responsibility centres, comparing actual results with them continuously and taking corrective action on deviations.

viva.q: How is the production budget derived?
viva.model: Budgeted sales plus desired closing finished stock minus opening finished stock.

viva.q: Why is a flexible budget better for control?
viva.model: Because it shows the cost allowed at the actual level of activity, so variances reflect efficiency rather than volume changes.
Actual hours worked divided by budgeted hours, expressed as a percentage.

viva.q: What is a decision package in ZBB?
viva.model: A description of an activity with its costs, benefits and alternatives, used to rank and fund activities from zero.

cases.title: Shine Detergents
cases.case: Shine Detergents budgets for Q1: sales Jan 8,000, Feb 10,000, Mar 12,000 packs at ₹50. Customers pay 60% in the month of sale and 40% next month (December sales ₹3,00,000). Closing stock of finished goods is to be 20% of next month's sales; opening stock on 1 January is 1,600 packs.

mcqs.explain: Sales 8,000 + closing 2,000 (20% of 10,000) − opening 1,600 = 8,400. In practice: link months.
60% × 5,00,000 + 40% × 4,00,000 = 3,00,000 + 1,60,000 = 4,60,000. In practice: lag creates working capital need.

mcqs.q: If actual sales differ from budget, the best control tool is:
mcqs.explain: Flexible budgets restate allowed costs at actual volume. In practice: revise monthly.
mcqs.topic: Fixed and flexible budgets; budget ratios
